1981 Classic Yacht Monaco Is a Priceless Gem for Today’s Gentleman
27 photos
Photo: Y.CO
A small, but elegant pleasure craft, the fully-refitted and lovingly maintained Monaco carries the nostalgia of the golden era of Gentleman’s yachts through the decades. In a world where monster megayachts share the same billionaire’s playgrounds with wooden sailing yachts and vintage motor yachts, the understated elegance of Monaco might seem too discrete to be noticed, yet it hides the prestigious status of the Feadship Heritage Fleet membership.
The tale of the Monaco yacht’s origin has gained the aura of a Viking legend over the decades, simply because of prosaic weather conditions. It seems that in 1981, the winter weather was so extreme that workers at the Dutch Kaag shipyard, who were bringing this Feadship to life, had to skate their way to the yard – a fairytale picture of the Monaco yacht being born.
Originally named Arkan, the winter-born new yacht also marked the beginning of a new phase in the evolution of Feadship design. To this day, Feadship yachts from the years prior to the 1980s flaunt the famous fantail stern. Arkan looks different, because the signature style was already beginning to change in the early ‘80s. However, it kept the covered aft deck, designed to be fully enclosed in bad weather conditions.
Photo: Feadship Boasting a slim silhouette of just under 125 feet (38 meters) with a 24-foot (7.2 meters) beam, Monaco was the spitting image of a graceful Gentleman’s yacht, the type of yachts that became popular around the mid-20th century for their understated elegance and noble spirit. Today, Monaco is endearingly referred to as “a petit Feadship”, in stark contrast to the contemporary mammoths delivered by this builder specializing in 50-to-100 meters long superyachts.
Quickly approaching its half-a-century anniversary, Monaco’s number of owners can be counted on the fingers of one hand. It first changed hands in the early ‘90s, when it was renamed Matanthar. Later, in the 2000s, it was renamed Monaco, still its name to this day, even though it seems to have changed ownership one more time. Prior to it being sold last month, Monaco had been with its last owners for more than 15 years, and says it all.
Millionaires who choose to invest in classic yachts , knowing full well that this often means further costs related to ample refits and overall maintenance, tend to be loyal to these old vessels and appreciate them for longer, not because they’ve put so much money into them, but because they seem them as collectors’ items. And Feadship gives them an extra reason to do so: becoming a member of the exclusive Heritage Fleet Club.
Photo: Pendennis As one of the most prolific and successful yacht builders in history, Feadship still counts hundreds of classic yachts still in operation today. That is why it has established The Feadship Heritage Fleet as an association for the owners of registered classic Feadships. The number one criterion is a proven age of at least three decades, but each yacht must be carefully confirmed and registered to become part of this exclusive club.
It’s not a cheap privilege. Following a €250 entry fee, members must pay an annual tax of €150 for yachts under 24 meters, and €500 for those over 24 meters. Membership comes with symbolic perks such as an official certificate and a stainless steel FHF logo that can be attached to the yacht, but what seems to matter the most is the companionship of like-minded owners and the ability to share personal experiences, tips about maintenance, and so on.
The Heritage Fleet wasn’t established on a whim. A dedicated research committee was set up a decade ago, in 2016, to work on a comprehensive archive of classic Feadships. There’s no other luxury yacht builder in the world to have a similar archive and Heritage Fleet, which demonstrates once again the immense historic value of these Dutch vessels.
Photo: Y.CO This is all to say that a yacht like Monaco, despite its humble size by today’s standards, is literally owning a piece of certified history. Just as important, the new owner is getting a pleasure craft in excellent condition, plus the benefit of a proven track record on the charter market. Monaco had less than a handful of owners in 45 years, and each one cared enough to invest in significant refits.
The acclaimed Pendennis shipyard alone has completed three of this refits, each during a different yacht ownership. The first one was in 1994. The second one, in 2005, was a more complex project that included a new bow-thruster, new switchboards, and a new distribution system. Beyond the technical upgrades, the newly-renamed Monaco received a fresh paint job, new teak decks, and an updated galley.
2016 was the year of the most comprehensive refit to this day. That is when Monaco’s Caterpillar D348 main engines were rebuilt to bring them back to zero hours. New generators were installed, and a complete exterior repaint ensured that the old yacht regained its former sparkle. All engineering systems were extensively upgraded during that seven-month refit, leaving the 1981 Feadship as good as new.
Photo: Y.CO To this day, the configuration and interior styling of the 124-foot Monaco prove to be versatile and popular. It’s highly unusual for a yacht this size to have both the master suite and the VIP suite on the main deck. It’s almost like having two master suites, and this is particularly welcomed by families during extended vacations. The two other suites are located on the lower deck, bringing the total number of guests that can accommodated to eight.
According to Feadship, skipping a fifth cabin, even if there was enough space for it, meant that all the four suites are very spacious, especially for a yacht this size. Together with crew quarters for up to seven members, this layout offers the benefits of a much bigger yacht with the footprint of an agile, more flexible 124-footer.
Although extensively refitted in terms of technical systems, Monaco hasn’t changed its classic style too much over time – even its hull color is the same as the original. The most noticeable addition to its amenities is a swim platform complete with aft stairs – no charter yacht can do without these things, and Monaco even carried a hefty toybox throughout its charter years.
Photo: Feadship The ingenious original configuration also included a wider range of outdoor options than you’d typically expect from a yacht in this size category. Guests have access to a small sunpad area on top of the wheelhouse, an observation lounge on the foredeck, and a generous area dedicated to al-fresco dining.
The original Terence Disdale interior design was discretely refreshed over time, but not dramatically changed. Guests can still admire the classic glossy mahogany that shows up in all Gentleman’s yachts, the traditional nautical theme in shades of cream and navy, and the formal dining spaces with a somber elegance. To some, this classic aesthetic might look a bit dated, but its suites the member of a classic yacht Heritage Fleet.
Proof of its enduring design and legacy, Monaco changed hands in October 2026, after being with its recent owners for more than 15 years. The last known asking price doesn’t reflect its true value: €3,9 million ($4.3 million), but the Heritage Fleet membership does.
